parts.partTitle: Stop Treating HTTP as a Dumb Pipe

beats.headline: Is your API returning 200 OK for errors?
beats.subline: Treating HTTP like a dumb pipe kills observability and breaks your cache.
beats.narration: If your API returns 200 OK for a NullPointerException, your monitoring dashboards stay green while your service is actually burning. Let's fix your API semantics.

beats.title: Richardson Maturity Model
beats.subtitle: From RPC tunnels to true REST

nodes.label: Level 0
nodes.detail: RPC Tunneling: Single URI, POST only

beats.narration: Most production APIs land at Level 2. We use HTTP verbs to signal intent and status codes to signal outcomes. Level 3 adds hypermedia links, but for most teams, Level 2 plus OpenAPI is the sweet spot.

beats.title: Bad vs. Good API Design
beats.narration: Stop tunneling actions through a single POST endpoint. Use the HTTP method that matches the operation. DELETE for removal, GET for reads, and POST for creation. It makes your API predictable for everyone.

beats.title: Mapping HTTP Semantics

steps.explanation: Always return the location header for new resources.
Signals successful deletion without sending an empty body.

beats.narration: Return 201 Created with a Location header when creating resources. For deletions, 204 No Content is the standard. It keeps your response payloads clean and your clients happy.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): How DispatcherServlet actually routes your traffic →
beats.narration: Level 2 is your baseline. In Part 2, we trace the request pipeline through the DispatcherServlet to see how Spring finds your controller methods.

parts.partTitle: Inside the Spring Web MVC Pipeline

beats.headline: How does Spring find your controller?
beats.subline: It isn't magic. It's a highly orchestrated pipeline starting at the DispatcherServlet.
beats.narration: Every request hits the DispatcherServlet. But how does it map that URL to your specific Java method? It's a multi-step journey through handlers and adapters.

beats.title: The Request Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: From Servlet Container to Controller
beats.narration: The DispatcherServlet hands off to a HandlerMapping to find your method. Then, the HandlerAdapter resolves your arguments and invokes your code. Finally, a MessageConverter turns your object into JSON.

beats.title: The Mapping Engine
beats.narration: At startup, Spring scans your controllers and builds a registry of paths. When a request hits, the HandlerMapping finds the exact method to run, ensuring your path variables and query params are correctly injected.

beats.title: Tracing the Pipeline
beats.caption: What happens when things go wrong?

lines.text: # Spring MVC logs the resolution chain

beats.narration: If you ever get stuck, set your logging to DEBUG. You'll see exactly which HandlerMapping matched your request and which converter was used to serialize your response body.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Why exposing JPA entities is a security nightmare →
beats.narration: You know the pipeline. In Part 3, we stop exposing JPA entities in our controllers and build immutable DTO records to prevent mass-assignment bugs.

beats.headline: Are you leaking your database schema?
beats.subline: Exposing JPA entities directly in your API is a massive security and stability risk.
beats.narration: Exposing JPA entities directly in your controller is a recipe for disaster. Mass assignment, serialization loops, and tight coupling—let's fix this with immutable records.

beats.title: Entity vs. DTO Pattern

top.label: Direct Entity

bottom.label: Record DTO
bottom.code:
public record UserDTO(String name) {}
public UserDTO get(...) { ... }

beats.narration: Never return your JPA entity. Use a Java Record as a DTO. It acts as an allowlist, protecting your internal fields like password hashes or audit columns from being serialized to the client.

beats.title: Jakarta Validation

steps.explanation: Ensures string is not null or empty.
Ensures quantity is greater than zero.

beats.narration: Use Jakarta Validation annotations on your records. Spring automatically triggers these when you add @Valid to your controller method. It's the cleanest way to enforce input constraints.

beats.title: Validation in Action
beats.caption: Catching invalid input early
beats.narration: When validation fails, Spring throws a MethodArgumentNotValidException. We catch this globally to return a clean, structured error message to the client, keeping our controller logic thin.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Standardizing errors with RFC 9457 ProblemDetail →
beats.narration: DTOs and validation are non-negotiable. In Part 4, we master global exception handling using RFC 9457 to standardize error responses across your entire microservice architecture.

beats.headline: Stop inventing custom error formats.
beats.subline: RFC 9457 is the industry standard for HTTP error payloads.
beats.narration: Stop inventing your own error JSON. Use ProblemDetail. It's the RFC 9457 standard, built into Spring, and it makes your API errors machine-readable for every client.

beats.title: GlobalExceptionHandler
beats.narration: Use @RestControllerAdvice to centralize your error handling. It keeps your controllers clean and ensures every exception returns the same structured ProblemDetail format.

beats.title: Legacy vs. RFC 9457
beats.narration: ProblemDetail is the standard. It includes status, title, and detail fields by default. It's what modern clients expect and what your infrastructure needs to correctly route and log errors.

beats.title: Enable ProblemDetail
beats.caption: One line in application.properties

lines.text: # Enable RFC 9457 for all MVC exceptions

beats.narration: Enable it in your properties file, and Spring will automatically convert built-in exceptions like 404s and 400s into RFC 9457 format. It's the easiest win for API quality.
